evidence.field: hanzi.etymology_notes[2]
evidence.text: 周所受瑞麥來麰。一來二縫，象芒朿之形。天所來也，故爲行來之來。《詩》曰：“詒我來麰。”凡來之屬皆从來。

evidence.field: hanzi.etymology_notes[3]
evidence.text:
Pictogram (象形) of wheat – original character of 麥 (OC *mrɯːɡ, “wheat”) or 麳 (OC *rɯː, “wheat”). The line in the middle represents the ear, the two lines pointing upwards represent leaves, and the lines pointing downwards represent the stem and roots. An additional horizontal line was often added at the top end of the character, possibly used to emphasize the ear of the wheat. Compare 禾; both are unrelated to 釆.
This character has been borrowed for “to come” since the oracle bone script. During the Western Zhou and Warring States periods, additional semantic components, such as 止 (“foot”) or 辵 (“to walk”), were added to differentiate the original sense from the borrowed sense. However, these additions were not inherited in later scripts.
Some consider the derivative 麥 from the addition of 夊 (“to walk slowly”) to be the original form for the meaning “to come”. If so, their meanings have interchanged due to frequent use of 來 for “to come”.
Shuowen connects “wheat” and “to come” from a mythological standpoint: 天所來也 (“it comes from the heavens”). This may be supported by archaeological evidence, which suggests that wheat is not native to China, but originated in the Fertile Crescent.
來 and 麥 have both been reconstructed to begin with *mr- in Old Chinese. The former retains the liquid as /l/, while the latter retains the nasal /m/.
From Proto-Sino-Tibetan *la-j ~ ra (“to come”) (STEDT). Cognate with 迨 (OC *l'ɯːʔ, “to reach; until”), 賚 (OC *rɯːs, “to bestow”), Burmese လာ (la, “to come”). Also cognate with 蒞 (OC *rɯbs, “to arrive”) according to Schuessler (2007). Unclear if connected to Vietnamese lại (“come; again”).

evidence.source: CUHK Humanum 漢語多功能字庫
evidence.field: 形義通解
evidence.text: Oracle-bone 來 depicts wheat: upright ear, drooping leaves, stem and roots. Both crop and movement uses occur early. Extra top strokes do not consistently distinguish the two uses. The exact relation with 麥 is debated.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫 — 來

evidence.source: CUHK Humanum 漢語多功能字庫
evidence.field: 來: palaeographic formation and component roles
evidence.text: The entry identifies oracle-bone 來 as a pictograph of a wheat plant, describing a central upright ear, drooping leaves, stem, and roots. It describes bronze forms as continuing the oracle-bone shape, sometimes with an added upper horizontal stroke. No phonetic component is proposed for 來 itself. The added stroke has been interpreted as distinguishing the wheat and movement uses, but the entry reports that oracle-bone examples do not show a consistent distinction; other proposals treat it as a decorative or redundant stroke, or as depicting the ear. These are source-reported analyses, not a visually verified reading of individual glyph images.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫 — oracle-bone component analysis: 來

evidence.source: CUHK Humanum 漢語多功能字庫
evidence.field: 來: competing accounts of the relation between wheat and movement senses
evidence.text: The entry’s main account is that the wheat graph 來 was borrowed for movement meanings and the loan became dominant. It also reports an alternative: 來 was borrowed for ‘come/go’ and given the semantic element 夊 in 麥 to mark movement, but that addition was later omitted from 來 for writing convenience; under this account 麥 eventually came to represent wheat. Thus the usual graphic/lexical history is disputed in direction, and the source does not establish the chronology solely from the graph’s shape.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫 — oracle-bone component analysis: 來

evidence.source: CUHK Humanum 漢語多功能字庫
evidence.field: 來: oracle-bone attestations and early movement uses
evidence.text: The entry cites oracle-bone examples for the movement reading, including 往來亡災 (‘going and coming, no harm’), 缶不其來見王 (H合集 1027正), and 來雨自西 (H合集 12872). It also notes uses glossed as ‘go,’ as in 王來正人方, and as ‘return.’ The entry treats these as phonetic-loan uses of the wheat graph. It does not assign individual inscriptions absolute dates in the inspected text, so their relative antiquity is clear as Shang oracle-bone material but a more precise date is not established here.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫 — oracle-bone component analysis: 來

evidence.source: CUHK Humanum 漢語多功能字庫
evidence.field: 來: oracle-bone wheat attestation
evidence.text: The entry identifies 乙亥卜，受來禾 (合集 33260) as a rare oracle-bone use of 來 for wheat, reading 來 as 麥 in a question comparing the harvest of wheat and millet/grain. It also records later bronze examples of 來 as wheat in its discussion of the related graph 麥, but does not date the cited items individually in the inspected text.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫 — oracle-bone component analysis: 來

evidence.source: CUHK Humanum 漢語多功能字庫
evidence.field: 來: semantic extension in oracle-bone and bronze usage
evidence.text: Beyond spatial movement, CUHK reports oracle-bone 來 used for tribute or bringing offerings (e.g. 奚來白馬, 合集 9177正) and for prospective time, including 來歲 ‘next year.’ It cites bronze uses for arrival, personal names, and 來歲. The entry proposes that the time sense extends the movement idea ‘from distant to near’; that is the entry’s semantic interpretation, not an independently dated chain demonstrating when each extension arose.

evidence.source: CUHK Humanum 漢語多功能字庫
evidence.field: 麥: semantic and phonetic role of 來; proposed graphic differentiation
evidence.text: For 麥, the entry analyzes 來 as the wheat-plant element and phonetic, with 夊 (related graphically to inverted 止) as a semantic addition associated with feet or movement. It says the added foot element was intended to distinguish the movement word, but long-term use of 來 for ‘come’ left 麥 to represent grain. This is an account of the related character 麥; it must not be transferred into a claim that 來 itself is phono-semantic.

evidence.field: 來: Shuowen explanation, seal form, readings, and dictionary senses
evidence.text: The Ministry entry reproduces the Great Xu Shuowen explanation: 周所受瑞麥來麰…天所來也，故為行來之來, with fanqie 洛哀切. It describes the seal form as resembling auspicious wheat. The entry lists Mandarin lái and lài; its lái senses include movement from elsewhere to here, temporal ‘up to now,’ occurrence, future/next, approximate quantity, and several grammatical uses. These are dictionary senses and examples, not proof of their chronological order. The Shuowen’s ‘heaven-sent’ explanation is a Han-dynasty account, not independent confirmation of the graph’s origin.

evidence.field: 來: Mandarin, Middle Chinese, and Old Chinese reconstructions by reading
evidence.text: In the authors’ 2014 Baxter–Sagart reconstruction dataset, both readings have modern Beijing lái and Middle Chinese loj (l- + -oj, level tone). ‘A kind of wheat’ is reconstructed *mə.rˤək (> *mə.rˤə); ‘come’ is *mə.rˤək (> *rˤə). Its introductory note says the MC notation represents pronunciation information from sources such as Guangyun rather than being itself a reconstruction.
